claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) has a five year survival rate below 10%
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is one of the most lethal human tumors, with a five year survival rate below 10% (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2020

claim: A subset of pancreatic tumors exhibit an 'adenosquamous' histology characterized by the presence of both glandular and squamous neoplastic cells within the same tumor
source: It has long been recognized that a subset of pancreatic tumors exhibit an 'adenosquamous' histology, which is characterized by the presence of both glandular and squamous neoplastic cells within the same tumor (Ishikawa et al., 1980; Morohoshi et al., 1983; Motojima et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical studies (Ishikawa et al., 1980; Morohoshi et al., 1983; Motojima et al., 1992)

claim: Approximately 15% of pancreatic tumor samples exhibit aberrant expression of squamous (basal) lineage markers, which is associated with exceptionally poor clinical outcomes
source: The designation of adenosquamous pancreatic cancer as a disease entity has been reinforced by several recent transcriptome profiling studies of human pancreatic tumors, which identified aberrant expression of squamous (also known as basal) lineage markers in ~15% of samples, in association with exceptionally poor clinical outcomes (Bailey et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Moffitt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptome profiling studies (Bailey et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Moffitt et al., 2015)

claim: Squamous cells are not known to be present in the normal human pancreas
source: While squamous cells are a normal cell type in several stratified epithelial tissues (e.g. in the skin and esophagus), they are not known to be present in the normal human pancreas (Basturk et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basturk et al., 2005

claim: The transcription factor p63 (ΔN isoform) is the master regulator of the adenosquamous phenotype in PDA
source: The functional relevance of squamous trans-differentiation in pancreatic cancer was unclear until recently, when studies from several laboratories, including our own, demonstrated that the transcription factor p63 (ΔN isoform, hereafter referred to as p63 for simplicity) is the master regulator of the adenosquamous phenotype in PDA (Andricovich et al., 2018; Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Andricovich et al., 2018; Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018)

claim: p63 binds to thousands of genomic sites to nucleate the formation of active enhancers to drive expression of squamous lineage genes in PDA cells
source: Once expressed, p63 binds to thousands of genomic sites to nucleate the formation of active enhancers to drive expression of squamous lineage genes (e.g. KRT5/6 and S100A2) in PDA cells (Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018)

claim: p63 is both necessary and sufficient to endow PDA cells with the same squamous lineage transcriptional program that is observed in pancreatic tumors with adenosquamous histology
source: Importantly, p63 is both necessary and sufficient to endow PDA cells with the same squamous lineage transcriptional program that is observed in pancreatic tumors with adenosquamous histology (Bailey et al., 2016; Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Bailey et al., 2016; Hamdan and Johnsen, 2018; Somerville et al., 2018)

claim: Induction of p63 leads to enhanced motility, invasion, and resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapy in PDA cells
source: In support of the functional impact of squamous trans-differentiation in PDA, induction of p63 leads to a collection of cell-autonomous phenotypic alterations, including enhanced motility, invasion, and resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapy (Danilov et al., 2011; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Danilov et al., 2011; Somerville et al., 2018)

claim: Inflammation has a powerful effect in driving PDA progression
source: Evidence from human patients and mouse models supports a powerful effect of inflammation in driving PDA progression (Cobo et al., 2018; Guerra et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2007; Yadav and Lowenfels, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Cobo et al., 2018; Guerra et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2007; Yadav and Lowenfels, 2013)

claim: Many pancreatic tumors are infiltrated with neutrophils, which suppress anti-tumor T-cell immunity in PDA mouse models and correlate with aggressive disease in humans
source: For example, many pancreatic tumors are infiltrated with neutrophils, which suppress anti-tumor T-cell immunity in PDA mouse models and correlate with aggressive disease in humans (Bayne et al., 2012; Chao et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2014; Steele et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Bayne et al., 2012; Chao et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2014; Steele et al., 2016)

claim: A subset of CAFs termed iCAFs have low expression of myCAF markers and produce high levels of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, such as IL-6, CXCL1, and LIF
source: Another subset of CAFs, termed iCAFs, have low expression of myCAF markers and instead produce high levels of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, such as IL-6, CXCL1, and LIF (Öhlund et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Öhlund et al., 2017

claim: Conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cell lines (BxPC3, T3M4, and KLM1) induced a distinct transcriptional response in pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) characterized by inflammatory gene expression
source: Remarkably, the PSCs within the Group 2 cluster were all treated with conditioned media derived from the three PDA cell lines expressing p63 (BxPC3, T3M4, and KLM1; Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing clustering of PSCs treated with conditioned media from p63-expressing cell lines, as shown in Figure 1E

claim: Conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cell lines led to a stronger induction of PSC proliferation than conditioned media collected from p63-negative lines
source: In addition to this transcriptional phenotype, the conditioned media from p63-expressing lines also led to a stronger induction of PSC proliferation than conditioned media collected from p63-negative lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase-based proliferation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: PSCs treated with conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cell lines showed significant enrichment of the iCAF signature
source: Using transcriptome data from our prior study in which we identified iCAFs and myCAFs (Öhlund et al., 2017), we defined gene signatures associated with these two cell fates (Supplementary file 2) and observed a significant enrichment of the iCAF signature within the Group 2 set of PSCs (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1H

claim: PSCs treated with conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cell lines showed significant enrichment of the myCAF signature within Group 1 PSCs
source: In contrast, the myCAF signature was significantly enriched within Group 1 PSCs (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1I

claim: Ectopic expression of p63 in SUIT2 cells enhanced cell growth when implanted into the mouse pancreas in vivo, but this phenotype was absent under tissue culture conditions
source: In a prior study, we found that ectopic expression of p63 in the human PDA cell line SUIT2, which lacks endogenous p63 expression, enhanced cell growth when implanted into the mouse pancreas in vivo, yet this phenotype was absent under tissue culture conditions (Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study (Somerville et al., 2018)

claim: Mouse PSCs cultured in SUIT2-p63 conditioned media showed a marked increase in iCAF markers (Il6, Cxcl1, and Lif) compared to those cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media
source: We observed a marked increase in iCAF markers (Il6, Cxcl1, and Lif) and a concomitant reduction of myCAF markers (Acta2 and Ctgf) when the PSCs were cultured in the SUIT2-p63 conditioned media compared to those cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B–C

claim: Mouse PSCs cultured in SUIT2-p63 conditioned media showed a concomitant reduction of myCAF markers (Acta2 and Ctgf) compared to those cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media
source: We observed a marked increase in iCAF markers (Il6, Cxcl1, and Lif) and a concomitant reduction of myCAF markers (Acta2 and Ctgf) when the PSCs were cultured in the SUIT2-p63 conditioned media compared to those cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Mouse PSCs cultured in SUIT2-p63 conditioned media were more proliferative compared to their counterparts cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media
source: In accord with the findings described above, mouse PSCs cultured in the SUIT2-p63 conditioned media were more proliferative when compared to their counterparts cultured in SUIT2-empty conditioned media (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase-based proliferation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: Conditioned media from KLM1 cells led to a significant induction of iCAF markers and repression of myCAF markers in mouse and human PSCs, and this effect was significantly attenuated in p63-knockout KLM1 cells
source: While conditioned media from KLM1 cells led to a significant induction of iCAF markers and repression of myCAF markers in mouse and human PSCs, this effect was significantly attenuated in p63-knockout KLM1 cells (Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–N).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–N

claim: p63 expression enhanced the growth of SUIT2 cells in vivo, but not in vitro
source: In accordance with our previous findings (Somerville et al., 2018), p63 expression enhanced the growth of SUIT2 cells in vivo, but not in vitro (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements and in vitro proliferation assays shown in Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: The transcriptional signature of iCAFs was significantly more enriched in the mouse stromal compartment of SUIT2-p63 relative to SUIT2-empty tumors
source: Importantly, the transcriptional signature of iCAFs was significantly more enriched in the mouse stromal compartment of SUIT2-p63 relative to SUIT2-empty tumors (Figure 3G), which is consistent with our conditioned media experiments (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: SUIT2-p63 tumors were more infiltrated with CD45+CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils when compared to control tumors
source: Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that SUIT2-p63 tumors were more infiltrated with CD45+CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils when compared to control tumors, which is a marker of enhanced tissue inflammation (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3H–I

claim: Plasma concentrations of the murine cytokine IL-6 were approximately 10 fold higher in mice bearing SUIT2-p63 versus SUIT2-empty tumors
source: Finally, plasma concentrations of the murine cytokine IL-6, a marker of systemic inflammation and immunosuppression (Flint et al., 2016; Nishimoto and Kishimoto, 2006) that is largely produced by iCAFs in PDA (Biffi et al., 2019; Elyada et al., 2019; Öhlund et al., 2017), were ~10 fold higher in the mice bearing SUIT2-p63 versus SUIT2-empty tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1U).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1U

claim: p63 inactivation in KLM1 cells resulted in a significant reduction in tumor growth when compared to control tumors
source: By monitoring tumor progression using bioluminescent imaging, we found that p63 inactivation resulted in a significant reduction in tumor growth when compared to control tumors (Figure 4A–B), which is consistent with in vivo-specific growth enhancement caused by acute p63 expression in SUIT2 and mM1 orthotopic models (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–K).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 4A–B

claim: Within the sorted fibroblast compartment, 396 genes were significantly downregulated in p63-knockout tumors, which included a significant suppression of the iCAF gene signature
source: Within the sorted fibroblast compartment, we identified 396 genes that were significantly downregulated in the p63-knockout tumors, which included a significant suppression of the iCAF gene signature (Figure 4H–J and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4H–J

claim: Within the sorted immune cell fraction, 463 genes were significantly down-regulated in p63-knockout tumors, which was enriched for markers of neutrophils, such as Ly6g, Mpo, S100a8, S100a9 and Cxcr2
source: Finally, within the sorted immune cell fraction we identified 463 genes that were significantly down-regulated in the p63-knockout tumors, which was enriched for markers of neutrophils, such as Ly6g, Mpo, S100a8, S100a9 and Cxcr2 (Figure 4I–K and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and ontology analysis shown in Figure 4I–K

claim: SUIT2-p63/PSC co-cultures released soluble factors that increased the chemotaxis of primary mouse neutrophils, and this phenotype was enhanced in the SUIT2-p63/PSC co-culture as compared to each cell type individually
source: We found that the SUIT2-p63/PSC co-cultures released soluble factors that increased the chemotaxis of primary mouse neutrophils and, importantly, this phenotype was enhanced in the SUIT2-p63/PSC co-culture as compared to each cell type individually (Figure 4M–N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 4M–N

claim: GSEA comparing SUIT2-p63 to SUIT2-empty cells revealed the activation of a number of inflammation-related pathways as top-ranking gene sets following p63 expression
source: GSEA comparing SUIT2-p63 to SUIT2-empty cells revealed the activation of a number of inflammation-related pathways as top-ranking gene sets following p63 expression (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: IL1A, IL1B, CXCL1, CXCL8, CSF2 (GM-CSF), CCL20, AREG, FJX1, and ADORA2B are the top inflammation-related genes regulated by p63
source: These analyses identified IL1A, IL1B, CXCL1, CXCL8, CSF2 (GM-CSF), CCL20, AREG, FJX1, and ADORA2B as the top inflammation-related genes regulated by p63 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: ChIP-seq analysis revealed that each of the top inflammation-related genes regulated by p63 is located near a p63-bound enhancer element
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by DNA sequencing (ChIP-seq) analysis performed in BxPC3 cells revealed that each of these genes is located near a p63-bound enhancer element, suggesting direct transcriptional regulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: ChIP-seq analysis revealed a p63-induced super-enhancer located at an intergenic region between the IL1A and IL1B genes
source: ChIP-seq analysis revealed a p63-induced super-enhancer located at an intergenic region between the IL1A and IL1B genes (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data and ROSE analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H

claim: CRISPR-interference targeting of the p63-bound enhancers at the IL1 locus was responsible for activating IL1A and IL1B expression
source: Using CRISPR-interference to target this region for inactivation (Qi et al., 2013), we verified that this group of p63-bound enhancers was responsible for activating IL1A and IL1B expression (Figure 5E–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data following CRISPR-interference shown in Figure 5E–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I

claim: ELISA experiments detected IL-1α, but not IL-1β, in conditioned media from KLM1 control cells, and the levels of secreted IL-1α were significantly reduced by two independent TP63 sgRNAs
source: This assay efficiently detected IL-1α, but not IL-1β, in the control setting and the levels of secreted IL-1α were significantly reduced by two independent TP63 sgRNAs (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Ectopic expression of p63 in SUIT2 cells led to robust secretion of IL-1α, but not IL-1β, and this effect could be ablated by CRISPR-interference-mediated targeting of the IL1 super-enhancer
source: Consistent with this observation, ectopic expression of p63 in SUIT2 cells led to robust secretion of IL-1α, but not IL-1β, and this effect could be ablated by CRISPR-interference-mediated targeting of the IL1 super-enhancer (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5H–I

claim: PSCs infected with control sgRNA displayed a marked increase in iCAF gene expression following culture in SUIT2-p63 conditioned media, but this induction was absent in IL-1 receptor knock out lines
source: Consistent with the results above, PSCs infected with the control sgRNA displayed a marked increase in iCAF gene expression following culture in SUIT2-p63 conditioned media (Figure 5J–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K). However, this induction was absent in the IL-1 receptor knock out lines (Figure 5J–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5J–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–K

claim: The expression of IL1A was significantly elevated in TP63high versus TP63low patient samples in three independent datasets
source: In all three datasets, the expression of IL1A was found to be significantly elevated in TP63high versus TP63low patient samples (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of three independent transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 6A

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq data confirmed that TP63 is aberrantly expressed in the ductal compartment of a subset of patient samples that exhibit high-level expression of squamous marker genes
source: We next interrogated single-cell RNA-seq data from 24 human PDA tumors and 11 normal pancreas tissue samples from a recently published study (Peng et al., 2019). This analysis confirmed that TP63 is aberrantly expressed in the ductal compartment of a subset of patient samples that exhibit high-level expression of squamous marker genes (Figure 6B–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Significantly higher expression of inflammatory genes (CXCL1, IL6 and LIF) was observed within the fibroblast compartment in TP63high versus TP63low patients
source: Importantly, we observed significantly higher expression of inflammatory genes (CXCL1, IL6 and LIF) within the fibroblast compartment in TP63high versus TP63low patients (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Multiplex immunofluorescence staining of 12 human PDA tissue samples revealed a trend towards increased neutrophil infiltration in p63-positive versus p63-negative PDA samples
source: Finally, we performed a multiplex immunofluorescence staining of 12 human PDA tissue samples, which revealed a trend towards increased neutrophil infiltration in p63-positive versus p63-negative PDA samples (Figure 6E–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by multiplex immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 6E–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: p63-expressing squamous PDA cells have an enhanced capability to promote inflammatory changes within the tumor microenvironment when compared to p63-negative PDA cells
source: Here we provide evidence that p63-expressing squamous PDA cells have an enhanced capability to promote inflammatory changes within the tumor microenvironment when compared to p63-negative PDA cells.
evidence: Supported by in vitro and in vivo experiments described throughout the manuscript

claim: p63 promotes enhancer-mediated transcriptional activation of genes encoding secreted factors with established roles in promoting inflammation
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that p63 promotes enhancer-mediated transcriptional activation of genes encoding secreted factors with established roles in promoting inflammation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing p63 binding at enhancers of inflammatory genes

claim: p63 activates a pro-inflammatory secretory phenotype that triggers iCAF induction through an IL-1-dependent signaling mechanism
source: Mechanistically, we have shown that p63 activates a pro-inflammatory secretory phenotype that triggers iCAF induction through an IL-1-dependent signaling mechanism.
evidence: Supported by conditioned media experiments, ELISA data, and IL-1 receptor knockout experiments

claim: A super-enhancer is installed by p63 at the IL1 locus, which enables a > 30 fold increase in IL-1α secretion to enhance iCAF formation
source: We account for this observation by demonstrating that a super-enhancer is installed by p63 at the IL1 locus, which enables a > 30 fold increase in IL-1α secretion to enhance iCAF formation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing super-enhancer formation and ELISA data showing increased IL-1α secretion

claim: IL-1/JAK/STAT signaling is the key pathway responsible for iCAF formation in PDA
source: We previously demonstrated that IL-1/JAK/STAT signaling is the key pathway responsible for iCAF formation in PDA (Biffi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study (Biffi et al., 2019)

claim: Many of the genes regulated by p63 in PDA cells correspond to those activated by the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB
source: Many of the genes regulated by p63 in PDA cells correspond to those activated by the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis showing enrichment of NF-κB signaling pathway

claim: p63 and NF-κB co-occupy a common set of target genes in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, and this is associated with enhanced inflammation in vivo
source: Indeed, it has been previously shown that p63 and NF-κB co-occupy a common set of target genes in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, and this is associated with enhanced inflammation in vivo (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2011

claim: NF-κB is often constitutively active in most pancreatic cancer tissues and confers resistance to apoptosis
source: In addition, NF-κB is often constitutively active in most pancreatic cancer tissues and confers resistance to apoptosis (Dong et al., 2002; Wang et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2002 and Wang et al., 1999

claim: Constitutive activation of NF-κB requires an IL-1α-driven feed-forward amplification loop to promote PDA development
source: In this context, constitutive activation of NF-κB requires an IL-1α-driven feed-forward amplification loop to promote PDA development (Ling et al., 2012; Niu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ling et al., 2012 and Niu et al., 2004

claim: Maintenance of an inflamed CAF state has been shown to be dependent on the NF-κB signaling pathway
source: Maintenance of an inflamed CAF state has also been shown to be dependent on the NF-κB signaling pathway (Biffi et al., 2019; Erez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biffi et al., 2019 and Erez et al., 2010

claim: p63 promotes expression of other pro-inflammatory cytokines that have been implicated in the development and progression of PDA, such as CXCL1 and GM-CSF
source: In addition to IL-1α, p63 promotes expression of other pro-inflammatory cytokines that have been implicated in the development and progression of PDA, such as CXCL1 and GM-CSF (Bayne et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; Pylayeva-Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citations to studies (Bayne et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; Pylayeva-Gupta et al., 2012)

claim: An association between squamous cell carcinomas and infiltrating inflammatory cells has been observed previously in other tumor contexts
source: An association between squamous cell carcinomas and infiltrating inflammatory cells has been observed previously in other tumor contexts (Andreu et al., 2010; Coussens et al., 1999; Erez et al., 2010; Eruslanov et al., 2014; Ferone et al., 2016; Kargl et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Squamous trans-differentiation in a lung adenocarcinoma mouse model was associated with neutrophil infiltration and other markers of inflammation
source: In one study, squamous trans-differentiation in a lung adenocarcinoma mouse model was associated with neutrophil infiltration and other markers of inflammation (Mollaoglu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollaoglu et al., 2018

claim: In lung adenocarcinoma, inflammatory changes were promoted by the squamous lineage transcription factor SOX2 through activation of CXCL5 expression
source: In this context, inflammatory changes were promoted by the squamous lineage transcription factor SOX2 through activation of CXCL5 expression (Mollaoglu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollaoglu et al., 2018

claim: Squamous cells of the epidermis are known to express large amounts of IL-1α at steady state
source: Notably, squamous cells of the epidermis are known to express large amounts of IL-1α at steady state (Hauser et al., 1986) and IL1A is known to be a key p63 target in normal human keratinocytes (Barton et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hauser et al., 1986 and Barton et al., 2010

claim: IL1A is a key p63 target in normal human keratinocytes
source: Notably, squamous cells of the epidermis are known to express large amounts of IL-1α at steady state (Hauser et al., 1986) and IL1A is known to be a key p63 target in normal human keratinocytes (Barton et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barton et al., 2010

claim: p63 points to a functional biomarker that identifies a poor prognostic subgroup of PDA patients in which inflammatory pathways are amplified
source: The findings presented in our study point to p63 as a functional biomarker that identifies a poor prognostic subgroup of PDA patients in which inflammatory pathways are amplified.
evidence: Supported by data showing correlation between p63 expression and inflammatory markers in patient samples

claim: Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-1α or IL-1β have shown promise as potential cancer therapies
source: For example, monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-1α or IL-1β have shown promise as potential cancer therapies (Hickish et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2014; Ridker et al., 2017), and the IL-1 receptor antagonist Anakinra has shown efficacy in pre-clinical models of PDA (Zhuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Hickish et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2014; Ridker et al., 2017; Zhuang et al., 2016)

claim: The IL-1 receptor antagonist Anakinra has shown efficacy in pre-clinical models of PDA
source: For example, monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-1α or IL-1β have shown promise as potential cancer therapies (Hickish et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2014; Ridker et al., 2017), and the IL-1 receptor antagonist Anakinra has shown efficacy in pre-clinical models of PDA (Zhuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhuang et al., 2016

claim: MIAPaca2 cells only express the TA isoform of p63 and lack expression of squamous lineage markers
source: Of note, MIAPaca2 cells only express the TA isoform of p63 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and lack expression of squamous lineage markers (Somerville et al., 2018), and in fact are more representative of a cell type of neuroendocrine origin (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to prior studies

claim: MIAPaca2 cells are more representative of a cell type of neuroendocrine origin
source: Of note, MIAPaca2 cells only express the TA isoform of p63 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and lack expression of squamous lineage markers (Somerville et al., 2018), and in fact are more representative of a cell type of neuroendocrine origin (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2019

claim: KLM1 is the only p63-positive PDA cell line identified which does not exhibit a growth arrest phenotype in vitro following p63 inactivation
source: Notably, KLM1 is the only p63-positive PDA cell line we have identified which does not exhibit a growth arrest phenotype in vitro following p63 inactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H; Somerville et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by competition-based GFP depletion assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H and citation to prior study

claim: KLM1 cells harbor a similar transcriptional and epigenomic profile as observed in other p63-expressing PDA cell lines
source: Importantly, KLM1 cells harbor a similar transcriptional and epigenomic profile as observed in other p63-expressing PDA cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–K).
evidence: Supported by GSEA and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–K

claim: The in vivo-specific growth advantage caused by ectopic p63 expression was validated in mM1 organoids following transplantation into the pancreas of C57BL/6 mice
source: Importantly, we validated the in vivo-specific growth advantage caused by ectopic p63 expression in the mM1 organoids following transplantation into the pancreas of C57BL/6 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–K).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements and in vitro proliferation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–K

claim: Orthotopic mM1-p63 tumors showed a decrease in infiltrating CD4- and CD8-positive T cells
source: Moreover, a similar neutrophil infiltration phenotype was observed in the orthotopic mM1-p63 tumors, which also correlated with a decrease in infiltrating CD4- and CD8-positive T cells (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J–K

claim: Tumor-associated neutrophils have an immunosuppressive effect in PDA
source: This finding is consistent with prior evidence that tumor-associated neutrophils have an immunosuppressive effect in PDA (Bayne et al., 2012; Chao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayne et al., 2012 and Chao et al., 2016

claim: iCAF induction and neutrophil infiltration were correlated with pre-existing levels of TP63 expression in human PDA organoid xenografts models
source: iCAF induction and neutrophil infiltration were also correlated with pre-existing levels of TP63 expression in human PDA organoid xenografts models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q–T).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q–T

claim: FACS of fibroblasts from SUIT2-p63 and SUIT2-empty tumors confirmed an increase in iCAF markers and a decrease in myCAF markers in the SUIT2-p63 tumors
source: However, fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS) of fibroblasts from these two groups of tumors confirmed an increase in iCAF markers and a decrease in myCAF markers in the SUIT2-p63 tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N–P).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from FACS-sorted fibroblasts shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N–P

claim: Reduced neutrophil infiltration in p63 knockout tumors was confirmed by immunofluorescence staining for LY6G and myeloperoxidase (MPO)
source: We confirmed reduced neutrophil infiltration in the p63 knockout tumors by immunofluorescence staining for LY6G and myeloperoxidase (MPO) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H

claim: SUIT2-p63 cells augmented the iCAF phenotype versus controls in a co-culture system with mouse PSCs
source: RT-qPCR analysis for murine-specific transcripts confirmed that SUIT2-p63 cells augmented the iCAF phenotype versus controls in this co-culture system (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I

claim: Conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cells could promote a modest degree of neutrophil recruitment in the absence of co-cultured PSCs, and this effect was dependent on CXCL1
source: Of note, we found that conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cells could also promote a modest degree of neutrophil recruitment in the absence of co-cultured PSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M). This effect was dependent on CXCL1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M), which is a p63 target gene in PDA cells (see below).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assays with CXCL1 blocking antibody shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M
